LLC MEMBER DISSOCIATION AND BUYOUT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This document states California's statutory default rules on member dissociation for Acme, Inc., a limited liability company formed under the laws of California: the events that cause a member of Acme, Inc. to be legally dissociated, the default legal effect of dissociation on that person's voting, management, and economic rights, and whether Acme, Inc. continues in existence afterward. It is a statement of the applicable statute's own default rules, not advice about how any particular member's dissociation should be handled. The members of Acme, Inc. remain free to adopt different rules in a written operating agreement to the extent the statute allows.

STATUTORY DISSOCIATION TRIGGERS
Under California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member of an LLC is legally "dissociated" — meaning that person's status as a member ends — on the occurrence of any of a specific list of statutory events. These include: the LLC's having notice of the member's express will to withdraw (or a later withdrawal date the member specifies); an event the operating agreement itself designates as causing dissociation; the member's expulsion under the operating agreement's own terms, by unanimous consent of the other members under specified circumstances (including an unlawful continuation with that member, a full transfer of the member's transferable interest other than for security or an unforeclosed charging order, or certain dissolution-related events for a corporate or entity member), or by judicial order on specified grounds (wrongful conduct materially affecting the LLC, persistent material breach, or conduct making it impracticable to carry on with the member); for an individual member, death or, in a member-managed LLC, the appointment of a guardian or conservator or a judicial finding of incapacity; in a member-managed LLC, the member becoming a debtor in bankruptcy; for a member that is a trust or an estate, distribution of that trust's or estate's entire interest (other than by a mere trustee or representative substitution); for any other non-individual member, the member's own termination; the LLC's participation in certain mergers where the member ceases to be a member; and the LLC's own termination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A person is dissociated as a member from a limited liability company when any of the following occur: (a) The limited liability company has notice of the person’s express will to withdraw as a member, but, if the person specified a withdrawal date later than the date the limited liability company had notice, on that later date. (b) An event stated in the operating agreement as causing the person’s dissociation to occur. (c) The person is expelled as a member pursuant to the operating agreement."
  — California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dissociation by express will to withdraw, agreed event, or agreement-based expulsion, Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.02(a)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17706.02)
  "(f) In the case of a person who is an individual, if either of the following applies: (1) The person dies. (2) In a member-managed limited liability company if either of the following applies: (A) A guardian or general conservator for the person is appointed. (B) There is a judicial order that the person has otherwise become incapable of performing the person’s duties as a member under this title or the operating agreement. (g) In a member-managed limited liability company, the person becomes a debtor in bankruptcy."
  — California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dissociation of an individual member by death and, in a member-managed LLC, by bankruptcy, Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.02(f)-(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17706.02)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory list of events that dissociate a member from a California LLC — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This is a distinct statute from the one governing dissociation of a partner from a California general partnership (the Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, cited elsewhere in this library under a different set of section numbers); LLC and general-partnership dissociation are separate statutory schemes in California, even though several of the underlying trigger events sound similar. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (Section 17706.02); they are not independent of one another.

POWER TO DISSOCIATE AND WRONGFUL DISSOCIATION
Under California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member always has the power to dissociate by express withdrawal, even if doing so is wrongful. Dissociation is wrongful only in specific circumstances the statute defines — chiefly, when it breaches an express provision of the operating agreement, or when it occurs before the LLC terminates and results from the member's own express withdrawal, judicial expulsion, becoming a debtor in bankruptcy, or (for an entity member) dissolving or terminating. A member who wrongfully dissociates is liable to the LLC and to the other members for any damages the dissociation causes, on top of any other debt, obligation, or liability the member already owes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A person has the power to dissociate as a member at any time, rightfully or wrongfully, by withdrawing as a member by express will pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 17706.02."
  — California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member's power to dissociate, Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.01(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17706.01)
  "A person that wrongfully dissociates as a member is liable to the limited liability company and to the other members for any damages caused by the dissociation."
  — California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, liability for wrongful dissociation, Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.01(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17706.01)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual default rule distinguishing a member's power to dissociate (which always exists) from the right to do so without liability (which is narrower) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. The statute's definition of "wrongful" dissociation lists several specific circumstances beyond the ones summarized here. All citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (Section 17706.01); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

EFFECT OF DISSOCIATION ON A MEMBER'S RIGHTS
Under California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, when a member is dissociated, three things happen by default: the person's right to vote or otherwise participate in managing the LLC ends; if the LLC is member-managed, that person's fiduciary duties as a member end going forward (though not for matters or events that arose before dissociation); and any transferable interest the person held as a member is thereafter held solely as a transferee — an economic-interest holder with a right to distributions, but without a member's voting or management rights. Dissociation does not, by itself, discharge the person from any debt, obligation, or other liability to the LLC or the other members that the person already incurred while a member.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "When a person is dissociated as a member of a limited liability company all of the following apply: (1) The person’s right to vote or participate as a member in the management and conduct of the limited liability company’s activities terminates. (2) If the limited liability company is member-managed, the person’ s fiduciary duties as a member end with regard to matters arising and events occurring after the person’s dissociation. (3) Subject to Section 17705.04 and Article 10 (commencing with Section 17710.01), any transferable interest owned by the person immediately before dissociation in the person’s capacity as a member is owned by the person solely as a transferee."
  — California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, loss of voting/management rights and transferee-only status on dissociation, Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.03(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17706.03)
  "A person’s dissociation as a member of a limited liability company does not of itself discharge the person from any debt, obligation, or other liability to the limited liability company or the other members that the person incurred while a member."
  — California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dissociation does not discharge pre-existing debts or liabilities, Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.03(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17706.03)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default status of a dissociated LLC member under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (Section 17706.03); they are not independent of one another.

DISSOCIATION DOES NOT ITSELF DISSOLVE THE LLC
Under California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, an LLC dissolves only on the occurrence of one of a specific, exhaustive list of statutory events: an event the operating agreement or articles of organization designate; a vote of members holding 50% or more of the voting interests (or a higher threshold the governing documents set); 90 consecutive days with no members at all; or a court's decree of judicial dissolution. An individual member's dissociation — by withdrawal, expulsion, death, bankruptcy, or any of the other triggers listed above — is not itself one of those listed events, so a member's dissociation does not by itself dissolve the LLC. The LLC continues by default with its remaining members unless the dissociation happens to coincide with one of the statute's actual dissolution triggers (for example, the departing member was the sole member) or the operating agreement designates that particular dissociation as a dissolution event.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A limited liability company is dissolved, and its activities shall be wound up, upon the happening of the first to occur of the following: (a) On the happening of an event set forth in a written operating agreement or the articles of organization."
  — California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, exhaustive list of statutory dissolution triggers, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.01)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's LLC act keeps a member's exit legally separate from the company's continued existence — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This citation is to a different, independently numbered section (Section 17707.01) than the dissociation-trigger and dissociation-effect sections cited above (Sections 17706.01-17706.03), so it is an independent source for this specific point.

NO GENERAL STATUTORY BUYOUT ON ORDINARY DISSOCIATION
California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act does not give an ordinarily dissociated member — one who withdraws, is expelled, dies, or is otherwise dissociated under the statute's dissociation-trigger list — a default statutory right to force the LLC or its remaining members to buy out that person's interest. The statute's own stated consequence of ordinary dissociation is that the person's interest continues to be held solely as a transferee, entitled only to distributions the LLC actually makes, with no built-in cash-out mechanism. The one buyout mechanism the statute does provide is narrower and different in kind: in a lawsuit for judicial dissolution, the other members may avoid dissolution by purchasing the suing member's interest for cash at its fair market value, with a court-supervised appraisal process if the parties cannot agree on that value. That mechanism is triggered only by a member's own lawsuit seeking judicial dissolution on specific statutory grounds — it is not a general buyout right that arises whenever a member dissociates.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "When a person is dissociated as a member of a limited liability company all of the following apply: (1) The person’s right to vote or participate as a member in the management and conduct of the limited liability company’s activities terminates. (2) If the limited liability company is member-managed, the person’ s fiduciary duties as a member end with regard to matters arising and events occurring after the person’s dissociation. (3) Subject to Section 17705.04 and Article 10 (commencing with Section 17710.01), any transferable interest owned by the person immediately before dissociation in the person’s capacity as a member is owned by the person solely as a transferee."
  — California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dissociated member holds interest solely as a transferee, Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.03(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17706.03)
  "In any suit for judicial dissolution, the other members may avoid the dissolution of the limited liability company by purchasing for cash the membership interests owned by the members so initiating the proceeding, the “moving parties,” at their fair market value."
  — California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, buyout limited to avoiding a judicial dissolution decree, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.03)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's current LLC act does not adopt a general default buyout right for a dissociated member's interest the way some other business-entity statutes (including California's own modern partnership statute, cited elsewhere in this library) provide fuller default buyout mechanisms for departing owners — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC, and not a claim that no other state's LLC statute provides a broader default buyout. The two citations below are to different, independently numbered sections (Section 17706.03 and Section 17707.03) and are independent sources for this point; note that the second citation describes a buyout tied specifically to a judicial-dissolution lawsuit, not to dissociation generally, and this document does not claim the statute provides any dissociation-triggered buyout beyond what these sections actually state.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
The undersigned member(s) of Acme, Inc. acknowledge that they have reviewed this statement of California's statutory default rules on member dissociation and the limits of the statutory buyout mechanism described above, and understand that Acme, Inc.'s own written operating agreement, to the extent state law permits, may adopt different rules governing dissociation events, a departing member's status, and any buyout of a departing member's interest.
